parts.title: Part 1 · Your neighbourhood
prompts: What do you like about the area where you live?
How often do you use public spaces near your home?
Has anything changed in your neighbourhood recently?
parts.sample: The thing I like most is how easy it is to do everyday errands on foot. There is a small market a few streets away, so I can pick up what I need on the way home and usually see someone I know.

parts.title: Part 2 · Cue card
prompts: Describe a public place you enjoy visiting.
Say where it is, when you go there and what you do there.
Explain why this place matters to you.
parts.sample: I'd like to talk about a small library near the river. From outside it looks like an ordinary office building, which is probably why I walked past it for years. I discovered it one afternoon when rain interrupted a long walk. Upstairs there was a reading room with tall windows looking straight over the water. These days I go there most Saturdays. I usually bring an essay I've been working on, because sitting somewhere quiet for an hour makes it easier to see which parts need rewriting. What makes the place special is that it serves people who use it quite differently. There might be a parent reading with a child downstairs, someone practising a language and a pensioner browsing the newspapers. I like how these routines share the same building without getting in one another's way. If the library closed, I could still read at home, but I would miss that sense of being connected to the neighbourhood.

parts.title: Part 3 · Public investment
prompts: How can public spaces help people from different backgrounds meet?
Should cities spend more on parks or on indoor community facilities?
How might technology change how people use public spaces?
parts.sample: I would start by looking at who struggles to use the facilities that already exist. A park may be the better investment where families lack safe outdoor space. In places with severe winters or where many residents live alone, an indoor centre may offer more consistent value. The decision comes down to which investment removes the biggest barrier to participation.
